sections.title: Letters and combinations
sections.content: Some Hungarian consonants are written with two letters. *sz* sounds like English s ("see"), while *s* alone sounds like English sh ("ship") — almost the opposite of what it looks like. *zs* sounds like the s in "measure", and *cs* sounds like English ch ("church"). *c* on its own, with no s, sounds like the ts in "cats". *gy*, *ny* and *ty* are all "wet"-sounding versions of *d*, *n* and *t* — press the middle of your tongue against the roof of your mouth, close to the d in "duke", the n in "canyon", the t in "tune". *ly* is a spelling leftover: today it's pronounced exactly like *y*. *j* is too — say it like the y in "yes", never like the English letter j. You can hold *sz*, *s* and *zs* on their own, so those play stretched out. The rest are best heard inside a word, so their rows play the word only.

One more habit worth building early: Hungarian always stresses the first syllable of a word. Unlike English, where stress hides — is it CONtent or conTENT? — Hungarian never makes you guess. Say every word like you're hitting a drum on beat one, and you'll already sound more confident than most learners.

*szia* does double duty as both "hi" and "bye" — Hungarian doesn't bother with two separate words the way English does. That's also why it can answer itself: *Szia!* → *Szia!* isn't an echo, it's just two people using the same all-purpose greeting in opposite directions.

For "thank you", *köszönöm* is the standard polite form. In everyday casual speech, it is very commonly abbreviated to *köszi* ("thanks"). You will also hear variations like *köszi szépen*, *kösz szépen*, or the even shorter *kösz* (and the colloquial *kösszer*) used for *köszönöm* among friends.
